rule: adjusted_score desc, total_score desc; dedupe by arXiv id / URL / id / title

papers.title: Generative Search and Recommendation at Shopify
papers.authors: Juhana Kangaspunta, Khalil Hajji, Darshan Fofadiya, Kyumin Park, Michael Garner, Anthony Maltsev, Ryan Synk, Jose Sepulv...
papers.summary: Search and recommendation at Shopify have to retrieve relevant products from a changing catalog of billions of items under tight latency limits. This report casts both tasks as generating semantic IDs: short sequences of content-derived tokens that represent products. The model is jointly pretrained on catalog and behavioral data so search and recommendation share a representation and a training objective. Reinforcement learning further improves judged search relevance, and distillation from task-specific experts improves recommendation without a statistically detected loss in search quality. In an online test on the home recommendation feed, adding the model raised attributed orders by 7.95%, converting users by 8.60%, and conversion rate by 9.85% on that feed.

papers.title: RedMall: Generative Recommendation for Large-Scale E-commerce
papers.authors: Kunyang Zhou, Xin Jia, Yi Yang, Yongjun Yang, Manjie Xu, Honglei Zhang, Yan Zhu, Kai Zuo, Xu Tang, Zheng Wang
papers.summary: Generative retrieval outputs a Semantic ID (SID), but several products can share one SID, and which of them are finally retrieved directly affects online gains. RedMall is a generative model for e-commerce recommendation and ad retrieval. Besides changes to the architecture and training objectives, such as treating items that were shown but not clicked as negatives, it handles this step explicitly. In serving, each product under the same SID gets a score, a weighted mix of the GMV it brought per thousand impressions in the past, weighted most, and its orders per thousand impressions, and only the top-scoring ones are kept. In the e-commerce recommendation A/B test, the full model raised GMV by 1.08%. The authors also tested this step on its own in ad retrieval: without it, the online lift in ad retrieval is no longer significant, because duplicates are filtered downstream and only about half as many items get through. ==How a SID is turned into products also decides how much generative retrieval gains==.

papers.title: TS-GEAR: Taobao Shangou GEnerative Ad Retrieval
papers.authors: Guofeng Tong, Xu Zhang, Guangliang Yu, Haiqiang Wang, Guannan Cong, Xing Guo, Yang Zhou, Jingjing Duan, Shuang Li, Feng ...
papers.summary: In food delivery search, a merchant that cannot reach the user's current location is not merely ranked low, it must not appear at all. Common SIDs are built only from content and collaborative signals and at best treat location as a soft signal, so unreachable merchants are filtered after generation, waste beam slots, and stay outside end-to-end training. TS-GEAR from Taobao Shangou writes location into the merchant ID: the first three tokens come from a geographic grid code, the last three carry content, and decoding restricts the first two tokens to the user's cell and its eight neighbors. At the production retrieval radius, 95.8% of its top 50 candidates are deliverable, while the strongest baseline, OneLoc, manages only a little over a third. ==A post-hoc filter can also delete bad merchants, but the surviving order never learned location==. In an online A/B test, ad revenue rose 4.2%. Teams building local-services retrieval can write this kind of hard constraint directly into the ID structure, so the model learns how to order merchants within reach.

papers.title: Not All Branches Are Equal: Adaptive Semantic ID Construction for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Guy Hadad, Haggai Roitman, Bracha Shapira
papers.summary: Generative recommendation numbers products with SIDs, and the dominant approach is residual quantization: each level has one global code table and looks up whatever the previous level left unexplained, which amounts to assuming that each token carries its own independent meaning. The authors checked RQ-VAE IDs on Amazon Beauty. Two products sharing only the first token have a mean cosine similarity of 0.740, while two that differ on the first token and share the last three reach just 0.582, about the same as a random pair. ==Later tokens have no stable meaning apart from their prefix==, so a SID is really a path in a tree. AST therefore builds the tree directly by clustering product embeddings from the top down, with each node choosing its number of branches by cluster quality. On five Amazon datasets it beats the strongest baseline by 13.08% on average, and because the methods share embeddings and the generative model, the gap comes only from how the IDs are built. For people building generative recommenders, this shows that rebuilding the IDs alone can pay off without touching the model.

papers.title: Rethinking Latent Reasoning for Generative Recommendation: Beyond Teacher-Generated CoT and Recurrent Hidden-State Feedback
papers.authors: Yiwen Chen, Fuwei Zhang, Zehao Chen, Deqing Wang, Hehan Li, Peizhi Xu, Hanmeng Liu, Shuanglong Li, Xin Pei, Fuzhen Zhuan...
papers.summary: Latent reasoning for generative recommendation usually needs a teacher model to write chain-of-thought traces, which is costly and hard to stabilize. This paper skips teacher generation. It builds semantic targets from the text meaning of items already in a user's history, and uses those targets to supervise the model's intermediate tokens that are reserved for reasoning steps, without looking at the next-item label. With supervised fine-tuning alone, the method outperforms the compared baselines across four recommendation benchmarks. On Beauty, it improves NDCG@1 by 20.6% and NDCG@5 by 10.3% over MiniOneRec. Controlled ablations indicate that the gain comes from input-matched historical semantic supervision, not from extra tokens by themselves.

papers.title: IntentLens: Grounding Underspecified Multimodal Queries for Recommendation via Tool-Augmented Reasoning
papers.authors: Xiao Chen, Dong Fang, Haitao Li, Qing Li
papers.summary: On devices such as smart glasses, users often give only a picture and one vague sentence, leaving style, budget and venue requirements unsaid. Existing recommenders either rely on past behavior or assume the request is already explicit, so direct similarity between query and candidates easily ranks the wrong places first. For example, a user points at a cafe dish and wants a similar vibe but a more affordable lunch. IntentLens adds a step before ranking: a multimodal LLM calls tools that inspect the image and search the user's history, then rewrites the vague request as an explicit text query. Candidates get details such as reviews and price before a lightweight two-tower model scores them. On the Google review data, holding the two-tower model and candidates fixed and changing only the query raises MRR from 33.6% to 40.2%, and the annotated reference query reaches 44.4%. ==The ranker stays the same, and the gain comes from filling in what the user left unsaid==. These queries are synthesized by LLMs, and each request takes several seconds. For search teams, this is a query-completion layer that can be added on its own before ranking.

papers.title: RecGroupMemory: Feedback-Aware Cohort Memory for E-Commerce Recommendation
papers.authors: Wendong Zhang, Weipeng Huang, Zhixin Ma, Bin Zhang, Dimin Wang
papers.summary: When a large model plans a recommendation workflow, it can be given memory of how a group of users has behaved. The difficulty is that new transaction feedback arrives the next day and the advice should change, while the record of the group definition, the observation window and the statistics must not be rewritten along the way. RecGroupMemory splits the memory in two layers. One is a read-only record of observations and the other is a profile with advice. The previous day's feedback may change only the second layer, and a check confirms the observations are unchanged, otherwise the original record is kept. In online comparisons on low-purchasing-power users chosen by the business team at an e-commerce platform, the group using memory alone had 1.58% more transacting users than its no-memory baseline. The group that added feedback revision had 1.78% more than its own no-memory baseline.

papers.title: LEGIT: Live Eligibility Gating over Identifier Tries for Constrained Decoding of Heterogeneous Pages
papers.authors: Felix Fang, Zheng Liu, Robert Saliba
papers.summary: Uber Eats generative search writes a whole page of stores and menu items in one decode, and every token must keep each store real, deliverable and unrepeated, with each item belonging to the store above it. These rules keep changing with the request and with what is already on the page, a trie over the catalog only keeps IDs real, and the grammar-constrained decoder the authors tried could not be both exact and fast. The authors compared dozens of implementations: the direct GPU version makes each token about 5 times as slow as unconstrained decoding, while the GPU compute units are active at most 5.42% of the time. Hardware counters and ablations both point to kernel launches and CPU waits on the GPU as the overhead. ==The arithmetic of the constraint is light, and the expense is the round trip to the GPU for each group of sequences==. Walking the trie on the CPU while the model runs its forward pass brings the cost down to about 1.7 times, with no custom kernel. Teams generating whole pages can keep per-token constraints on the CPU, as the authors suggest.

papers.title: RoutingTrie: Metadata Routing for Constrained Generative Retrieval
papers.authors: Darshan Fofadiya, Yang Liu, Shuying Sun, Kyumin Park, Juhana Kangaspunta
papers.summary: Generative retrieval often has to honor a condition, such as returning only products from one shop, while a trie only guarantees that a generated SID exists and says nothing about shops or countries. The usual approach filters after generation, but by then the beam is full of other shops' candidates and few results may survive. RoutingTrie moves the filter ahead of beam selection at every step: each edge of the SID trie records which shops, countries and other values occur below it, and decoding first blocks branches that cannot reach the requested value. Fields with few values are stored as bitmaps and fields with millions of values, such as shop ID, as sorted lists. Replaying historical purchases through a production system with a shop filter raises Hit@100 from 67.5% to 96.1% and adds only 1.1 ms of request latency. ==The model scores are unchanged, so the gain comes from no longer wasting the beam==. Teams running filtered retrieval can move metadata conditions into decoding without changing the model, although a finite beam still cannot guarantee that nothing is missed.

papers.title: CascadeRec: Deployed Adaptive LLM Compute Allocation for Multi-Tenant Content Recommendation
papers.authors: Kai Zhao, Guilin Zhang, Xiang Cheng, Xiquan Cui, Henry Heng, Xu Chu, Alet Blanken
papers.summary: Large language models are attractive rerankers, but running an expensive model on every request is costly and often hurts users with short histories. This production system, deployed for content recommendation at a large financial-planning software provider, reranks every request with a lightweight first tier. A router then uses segment cues such as history length to escalate only the requests more likely to benefit to a more expensive second tier, such as a larger model or multi-path reasoning. In a production experiment lasting over a month, it cut inference cost by about 10% versus using the expensive tier uniformly, with little latency impact and no observed quality regression. On MovieLens-1M and Amazon Electronics, uniform LLM reranking lowers NDCG@10 for sparse-history users by up to 30%, and the only statistically significant gain appears among users with the longest histories.

papers.title: Request-Only Optimization for Recommendation Systems
papers.authors: Liang Guo, Wei Li, Lucy Liao, Huihui Cheng, Rui Zhang
papers.summary: Recommendation training samples are usually cut per impression. One request sends the user several items, each impression becomes a sample, and the same user's features and long behavior sequence are copied into every one of them. Meta counted three of its products and found 4 to 7 impressions per request on average. ROO packs all impressions from one request into a single sample, so user-side features are stored once and computed once. The saved compute can go straight into a bigger user-side model. For retrieval, the offline gain that impression-level HSTU bought with 6.8 times the compute is reached with almost no extra compute per sample once training is per request. ==Long-sequence models are expensive largely because they recompute the same user==.

papers.title: STCRank: Spatio-temporal Collaborative Ranking for Interactive Recommender System at Kuaishou E-shop
papers.authors: Boyang Xia, Ruilin Bao, Hanjun Jiang, Jun Wang, Wenwu Ou
papers.summary: In a full-screen e-commerce feed where each swipe down brings the next item, the two ranking objectives of whether the user buys and whether they keep swiping fight each other. Kuaishou E-shop's data show that after a purchase, users leave right away without swiping 61.3% of the time. With the usual labels, every one of those purchases becomes a negative sample for the swipe objective, so the learned swipe score ends up pushing down the items that sell. The authors drop purchase-then-exit samples from the swipe negatives. Ranking also stops picking the top-scoring item one screen at a time. Instead it scores different orderings of the next few items: each item's value is multiplied by the probability that the user swipes far enough to reach it, and the ordering with the highest total wins. Adding this look-ahead ranking to the full-screen feed alone raised online purchases by 2.10%. Teams running immersive feeds should check their objectives for conflicting labels first.

papers.title: SepLRM: A Foundation Model Paradigm for Recommendation
papers.authors: Di Chen, Xijun Xiao, Qin Ren, Weijiang Lai, Zhijian Pan, Zhentao Pan, Pengfei Nie, Cheng Yuan, Zixuan Tan, Xuyang Liu, T...
papers.summary: On recommendation platforms, large models for different stages and business lines each encode the same long user history, and this repeated cost gets harder to justify as models and sequences multiply. Existing sharing schemes mostly pass downstream scores or compressed user representations, so the detail is already gone. ByteDance's SepLRM has one foundation model run the encoder and store the final representation of every behavior as a KV cache, and each downstream model builds queries from its own candidates and context to read it. Because the cut sits between encoder and decoder, downstream computation matches the end-to-end model, and without compression about 100% of the AUC gain from long sequences is preserved. ==A high AUC on the foundation model does not mean its exported cache is useful==, since encoder-only and decoder-only structures keep only about ninety percent downstream. Online, ROI in two scenarios reaches 8.62 times and 2.62 times that of matched end-to-end models, so investment in sequence modeling can be spread across many models.

papers.title: Exploiting Feature-invariant Scaling Laws for Efficient A/B Experimentation in Recommendation Systems
papers.authors: Zhiliang Chen, Sammy Nammari, Jiahao Su, Xiaoqiang Luo
papers.summary: Add a feature or change the architecture of a recommendation model, and a small-scale experiment may say it does nothing, while full-scale training shows it helps. The Meta authors hit exactly this on an LLM recommender: adding movie genres to the prompt lowered HR@10 at small scale and clearly raised it at full scale. They found that, whether a change helps or hurts, the model's validation loss follows the same power law as training scale grows, only with different coefficients. So they run a few experiments at reduced scales, fit the curve, extrapolate to full scale, and compute the probability that the new feature beats the baseline there. Together these experiments cost about 55% of one full-scale training run. ==A single small experiment misleads, but a curve of small experiments is quite reliable==. Across more than 40 changes to Wukong, HSTU and LLM-based recommenders, the method separates beneficial changes from neutral and harmful ones.

papers.title: Proactive Dimension-Adaptive Denoising for Graph Collaborative Filtering via Representation Coherence
papers.authors: Wenjun Li, Dong Zhao, Jiaying Shi, Juan Zhang, Zhaoming Pan, Zhimin Zhang
papers.summary: Implicit feedback mixes in accidental clicks and impulse purchases, and existing denoising methods almost all use training loss to find noise, but loss only grows after the model has been misled and is also disturbed by training stage and negative sampling. NDL from NetEase adds a signal that ignores predictions: the cosine similarity between an interaction's representation and the mean representation of that user's past interactions, where larger deviation means more suspicion, and ==this signal is available before the model makes a prediction error==. Active users rely mainly on this signal, while cold-start users with little history fall back to training loss. The fused suspicion score decides how many embedding dimensions an interaction may use, with more suspicious interactions getting fewer instead of being dropped outright. On public datasets where ratings below three count as noise, Recall@5 beats the strongest baseline DAR by 5.63% to 17.95%, with larger gains on sparser data. The change lives only in training and serving keeps LightGCN embeddings of the same shape, so integration is cheap, although the method has not yet been deployed online.

papers.title: SeqFold: Timestamp-Addressable Compressed States for User Action Sequence Backbones
papers.authors: Mianwei Zhou, Duo Zhang, Henry Tsai, Yuqi Zheng, Jian Li, Juexin Lin, Sujay Khandagale, Vijay Rajaram, Dong Jiao, Tao Ch...
papers.summary: Downstream search and recommendation models all want to reuse the output of a frozen long-sequence user model, but the full multi-layer hidden state for one user at one point in time averages several million bytes, too much to store or ship. Coupang's SeqFold compresses each layer's hidden states into a fixed number of interest slots: a learned gate decides how much each past action puts into each slot, older actions are decayed more, and each slot is finally quantized into a short binary code. Downstream models fetch the code for the moment before a target timestamp and decode it into their own embedding with a task-specific decoder. Storage shrinks by 3,400 times, and the uncompressed full version is only 2.11% better. ==Learning what to keep before compressing beats simply truncating to the latest actions by a wide margin==. Keeping only the latest 64 actions takes more storage and performs even worse.

papers.title: OptiCover: A Scalable and Multi-Surface Framework for Cold-Start Visual Optimization under Semantic Constraints
papers.authors: Guillaume Guy, Mihajlo Grbovic, Joe Mills, Selen Uguroglu, Liwei He, Pratiksha Kadam, Nalini Kartha, Qian Aria Li
papers.summary: Airbnb wants to choose cover photos for hosts, and there are two difficulties. Over 90% of listing photos have never been a cover and so have no click data to learn from, and the most clickable photo may show a nearby attraction that does not represent the listing. The authors first screen candidates with indirect cues, use a VLM to check photos against the listing description, and then pick by predicted CTR, which raises HomePage CTR by 1.5%. The more interesting part is a pair of experiments on Search. Picking the photo with the highest predicted clicks raises CTR significantly but leaves bookers without a significant change, and the extra clicks mainly move bookings from one listing to another. Narrowing candidates by the guest's filter, such as pools, before choosing leaves CTR without a significant change but raises bookers significantly by 0.35%, although the lower end of the confidence interval sits close to zero. ==On Search, narrowing candidates by guest intent brings more bookings than pushing up clicks==. Creative optimization cannot look only at clicks.

papers.title: SAGE-PAIR: Source-Pretrained Routed Residual Adaptation for Sparse-Feedback Recommendation
papers.authors: Weiqing Zeng, Zida Yang, Guquan You, Jiexin Zheng, Cong Wang
papers.summary: When a recommender moves into a new serving window, the target window often has too little feedback to retrain the live model. This paper freezes the original model and adds only a residual: the item features are click and like rates in the source window (exactly two dimensions), and the expert basis is a small set of anchors in that same plane. A soft router weights those anchors from the user's source-window behavior profile, and the extra term added to the original score is the inner product of the item features with that mixed direction. Scarce target feedback only updates these residual parameters. On a locked KuaiSAR-v2 test split, the full method raises NDCG@10 by 1.77% relative. Adding the routed experts gives a further 0.25% relative gain over source-pretrained residual adaptation without routing. When feedback is sparse, whether an update direction can be estimated may matter more than how many labels there are.

papers.title: Query- and Candidate-Aware Long User Sequence Modeling for Sponsored Product Ranking in Search
papers.authors: Dongyue Xie, Sergey Kolbin, Manavender Malgireddy, Iurii Shcherbak, Weixing Tang, Arushi Jain, Wanchen Shao, Kurt Zimmer...
papers.summary: When sponsored search ranking uses long-term behavior, the usual approach searches history for actions similar to the candidate product, which can miss history highly relevant to the current query but only loosely tied to the candidate. Beyond recent behavior, Wayfair retrieves one batch of long-term actions by candidate and another by query, then feeds them to a Transformer with two context tokens for the query and the candidate. Offline, the two retrieval channels together give a larger AUC gain than either alone, which suggests the history they find is complementary. Another finding is that injecting the candidate into every history token cannot be skipped, since removing it makes the model clearly worse than the production baseline, and ==a single global candidate token with indirect interaction cannot make up for it==. In an online A/B test of the full model, CTR rose 6.0%, orders per impression rose 11.5%, and model serving latency increased by about 12%. For long sequences in search, the query deserves its own retrieval channel, and token-level interaction between candidate and history should stay.

papers.title: INTENT: Out-of-Sample, Out-of-Time, and Cold-Start Evaluation on User Event Sequences
papers.authors: Mattias Kvist, Erik Lidman Hillbom, Edoardo de Cal, Davis Siemens, Adam Fredriksson, Rickard Brüel-Gabrielsson
papers.summary: Once deployed, sequence models in banking and recommendation face a period after the training cutoff, users never seen in training, and newly appearing items, yet the usual evaluation just holds out each user's last few events. INTENT splits the test into seven cells by whether each of these three was seen in training, and picks the cutoff date on five public datasets with one rule fixed in advance. Which model wins depends on the cell: SASRec leads on seen items but scores zero on new ones, while a training-free method that simply ranks the user's previous item first leads on new items in most datasets. New users cost almost nothing, while crossing the cutoff costs a lot. Using the training-free method as a control shows that, on three datasets, ==most of the drop comes from user behavior itself changing, not from the model failing to learn==.

papers.title: Beyond Ranking: Are Decision Models Calibrated Relevance Scorers?
papers.authors: Shengyao Zhuang, Xueguang Ma, Matthias Petri, Jimmy Lin
papers.summary: Decision models such as Jev generate no text and output a probability for each relevance level directly, and the vendor promises those probabilities are calibrated, yet earlier independent checks never compared them with graded human judgments. Checked against TREC human judgments, only 66% of the documents it scores above 0.9 are actually relevant, and the other models tested are too optimistic as well. The error is mostly one of scale, so a two-parameter Platt calibration fitted on one year of labels corrects much of it on a new year and a new corpus. With calibrated probabilities, choosing how many documents to keep per query by expected F1 needs no tuned threshold, matches a threshold tuned for the job, and clearly beats a fixed top-ten cut. On corpora from other domains the same calibration is less steady, helping some and hurting others. ==Ranking well does not mean the probabilities are right==, so anyone truncating RAG context by probability needs at least one set of their own human labels to calibrate against.

papers.title: Yuanbao-Reranker: Document-Grounded Synthesis and Preference Distillation for Text Reranking
papers.authors: Hongyuan Xu, Dezhi Ye, Jiahao Cao, Jie Liu, Haijin Liang, Haibo Shi, Jin Ma
papers.summary: Rerankers fine-tuned pointwise on relevant and not-relevant labels have a gap: every negative for a query carries the same label, so the model never learns which negatives sit closer to the positive. Tencent's Yuanbao Search pairs each positive with three negatives of different difficulty and adds a distillation loss: the teacher's score gap between two documents acts as a lower bound, and the student stops being penalized once it reaches that distance. On groups held out from training, the share with all three negative tiers ordered correctly rises from 36.4% to 69.7%, while separating positives from negatives was already near perfect. Replacing the lower bound with squared error that chases the gap scores below having no such loss at all, because gaps already opened get pushed back. ==The order among negatives is the information binary labels leave out==, the final 4B student beats the 8B model that taught it on the five-benchmark average, and when training a reranker it is worth checking first whether negative scores are bunched together.

papers.title: Lightfoot: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Exact, Model-Free Document Deletion
papers.authors: Uday Allu
papers.summary: GraphRAG in production has two costs that papers rarely count: what it takes to build the graph, and how painful it is to delete a document. When a contract expires or a user asks for erasure, a document and everything derived from it must go, yet entity summaries that blend several documents are hard to take apart. Lightfoot requires every record in the graph to be computed only from single-passage extractions, with one model call per passage, none at retrieval, and deletion as a plain database operation, and its index is also the cheapest on all three datasets. After deleting 10% of the documents on the full MuSiQue corpus, the graph is identical to a fresh index of the survivors, while LightRAG needs 2,187 model calls and 3.7 hours to delete the same documents. The price is accuracy that trades wins with HippoRAG 2 and falls clearly behind on 2WikiMultiHopQA. ==Exact deletion works because no record comes from a model call that read several passages==, and teams with compliance deletion needs can design their index around that constraint.

papers.title: Beyond Query-Item Matching: Personalized Behavioral Relevance Modeling for E-commerce Search via Rubric-Guided Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Yang Liu, Chenxu Wang, Jianzhi Shao, Jun Ji, Xiaozhou Xu, Zhe Sun, Wei Hu
papers.summary: E-commerce search usually has a relevance model sort candidates into tiers by text match between query and item, then hands them to a CTR model, so an item the user clearly prefers can get little exposure just because it landed in a low tier. This work from Alibaba's 1688 moves part of personalization into the relevance step: an LLM reads the user's same-day, recent and long-term search and purchase records, judges whether the item is backed by behavioral evidence, and if so promotes it one relevance tier. Training rewards not only the correct decision but also, through grading criteria generated for each sample, whether the reasoning actually uses that behavioral evidence. A three-day A/B test on 5% of main search traffic raised transaction-related user-days by 0.67%. ==Personalization need not live only in the ranking layer; changing relevance tiers also works.== Online serving only reads cached results computed offline, adding almost no latency.

papers.title: SPARSEUP: Towards Better Recipes for Training Modern Learned Sparse Retrievers
papers.authors: Thibault Formal, Pierre Erbacher, Cosimo Rulli
papers.summary: Sparse retrievers like SPLADE, moved onto newer backbones such as ModernBERT, often train poorly, and RoBERTa does not train at all. The authors trace this to the starting point: most of the new backbones' vocabulary scores are already positive, so at the start of training almost every term is active, the document representation is dense, and the gradient that tells terms apart weakens. The fix has three steps. Before training, one constant is subtracted from all scores, set at a high percentile of the score distribution estimated on a small sample of documents. Each input position may activate at most 12 terms. Case and word-boundary variants of the same word are merged. The final model reaches 56.4 average nDCG@10 on BEIR, only 1.5 points below a dense model trained on the same backbone and data. Anyone moving sparse retrieval to a new backbone can start with these three steps.

papers.title: Calibrating Document-Local Boundaries for Contextual Chunk Retrieval
papers.authors: Yuanxiang Wang, Hui Jiang, Da Zhu, Zhihua Chang
papers.summary: Late Chunking encodes a whole document before splitting it, which preserves context but makes similar chunks of the same document harder to tell apart, such as one player's scoring records from different seasons. On InSeNT, a baseline fine-tuned with same-document negatives, 82.21% of the failed queries have another chunk of the same document scoring above the correct one. DcLBC from Alibaba's Qwen team changes two things. It scales a query's scores up more when the correct chunk leads the highest-scoring wrong chunk of the same document by less, and it tells the attention layers during encoding where the chunk boundaries are. Neither change touches the embedding dimension or the retrieval procedure. Split into four tiers by same-document competition, the NDCG@10 gain concentrates in the hardest tier at 5.46 points, while the two easiest tiers barely move. ==Many long-document retrieval errors come from telling apart chunks of the same document==, so passage retrieval teams should count this kind of error separately.

papers.title: CoRA-Bench: Evaluating Evidence Preservation by Context Selectors Under Token Budgets
papers.authors: Huzaifa Pardawala, Siddhant Sukhani, Sudheer Chava, Agam Shah
papers.summary: Filtering content before long-context inference saves tokens, but it can also throw away the evidence the answer needs, and truncation, retrieval and compression have lacked a common way to be compared. CoRA-Bench compares truncation, BM25, dense retrieval, reranking and two compression methods under the same token budgets, computing evidence recall and answer accuracy on the same selected text, and no method wins everywhere. On NoLiMa, where evidence and question share little wording, dense retrieval reaches 0.908 evidence recall against 0.467 for BM25, and on BABILong, with explicit surface cues, BM25 leads instead. Keeping evidence is not the same as answering correctly either: under verbatim scoring Provence, which alters the text, keeps almost no complete evidence on LongMemEval, yet its answer accuracy is 66.60%. ==When choosing a context selector, look at evidence recall and answer accuracy separately==, and teams doing long-document QA or memory retrieval can pick a method by whether their evidence relies on literal matches or semantic association.

papers.title: NIFT-SQL: Customer-Supervised Table Scoring for Enterprise Text-to-SQL Retrieval
papers.authors: Arjun Rao, Nishant Gopinath
papers.summary: The first step of enterprise text-to-SQL is finding the tables, yet schemas often offer only cryptic table and column names, a query needs every table it joins, and generic retrieval struggles here. NIFT-SQL trains separately on each customer's example questions, has a small cross-encoder judge for every table whether it is needed, and fuses that with hybrid search over a retriever fine-tuned the same way. On LiveSQLBench-Large, with nearly a thousand tables, the share of questions with every needed table in the top fifteen is 21.8% for hybrid search without fine-tuning and 85.6% for NIFT-SQL, while the fine-tuned retriever alone reaches 70.4%. The lead is not stable: on a newer BEAVER release, trained only on synthetic questions, it loses to the fine-tuned retriever on real questions. ==With labeled questions in hand, a fine-tuned retriever is itself a cheap and strong baseline==, and the scorer adds the most when only a few tables fit in the context.

papers.title: PatternBloom: Empowering Agentic RAG with Externalized RL-Distilled Graph Patterns
papers.authors: Yi Ge, Heng Huang
papers.summary: RAG agents trained with reinforcement learning can learn to fetch better content, yet the steps for reasoning through a given type of question are worked out from scratch every time, and methods that retrieve only content plateau as questions get deeper. Asking which country the directors of two different films were born in follows the same steps: film, director, country. PatternBloom abstracts high-scoring reasoning runs into templates that keep only entity types (the paper calls the store Graph Pattern Memory). There are 27 of them, kept outside the model and looked up first so evidence is gathered along them. On five datasets unseen in training, the 7B version averages 49.0 EM, while Search-R1, the best trained method of the same 7B size, reaches 38.1. ==Reasoning paths that recur across multi-hop questions can themselves be the thing you retrieve==. Teams building agent search can turn the query steps of common questions into templates people can read and edit, though these experiments all use Wikipedia corpora.

papers.title: Search-by-Answer Bias in Retrieval Models
papers.authors: Adiel Avigad, Shauli Ravfogel, Yoav Goldberg
papers.summary: Dense retrieval should find passages by the relation a query asks about, but retrieval models carry world knowledge, and this paper shows they lean toward answers the model already knows, which can penalize rarer or newer answers. The authors build sentence pairs, one kind changing only the answer entity, the other pairing a right-relation sentence holding an alternative answer with a wrong-relation sentence holding the familiar answer. Across eight retrievers, the higher the probability a model gives an answer, the higher it scores passages containing that answer. On examples where the model already favors the canonical answer, Qwen3-Embedding-8B picks the familiar sentence 94.6% of the time when only the answer differs, against 50% with no bias, and ranks the wrong-relation sentence first 65.0% of the time. ==For queries with several valid answers or answers that go stale, retrieval is easily pulled toward what the model remembers==. The test sentences come from templates, but on QAMPARI, whose questions have many valid answers, the retrievers also favor the known answer.

papers.title: RecoGEM: A Serving System for Production-Scale Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Xiangrui Yang, Yunfeng Zhao, Jiawei Yang, Fangyu Zhang, Enrui Zhao, Liang Zeng, Cheng Peng, Minhui Xie, Jiaqiang Liu, Xi...
papers.summary: Generative recommendation has the model generate an item's SID token by token like an LLM, so LLM serving stacks look reusable, yet they run poorly because they assume every step has the same shape and attention cost sits in long sequences. This Kuaishou paper on RecoGEM spells out the difference: each candidate reads only a few SID tokens, but beam expansion creates a huge number of independent short sequences, so the fixed overhead of long-sequence kernels cannot be spread out. Every step also has its own vocabulary and tensor shape, and top-k must pick a large set of survivors after each step, which makes it heavy work on the critical path. The team hands candidate state between steps and live updates to a separate runtime, and compiles the engine for the shape of each step. On the production OneModel workload, one serving instance exceeds 1000 QPS with P99 below 35 ms, and throughput is 2.88 times that of the same system with a uniform shape and ordinary kernels. ==To cost out generative recommendation, look at beam width and candidate selection, since sequence length is not the main expense.==

papers.title: Firepool: Brokering Warm GPU Capacity for Agentic and RL Workloads at LinkedIn
papers.authors: Ankit Goyal, Santosh Jha, Zhuo Zhi, Youmin Han, Cong Gu, Chen Xie, Animesh Singh
papers.summary: Agents and RL training issue thousands of GPU jobs that run for seconds, yet starting a Pod takes twenty to thirty seconds even with the image cached, so waiting outweighs the work. Common fixes each miss something: caching images does not remove scheduling and initialization, a persistent Ray cluster holds GPUs idle between steps, and a warm pool of ready Pods often goes unused because the next job needs a different environment. LinkedIn's Firepool has Pods of one hardware profile share a base image and installs code and dependencies only when a job starts, which makes Pods interchangeable. For isolation, a Pod is reused only for the caller that last used it, and when the caller changes, a standby Pod on the same card that holds no GPU memory takes over. During a sampled production peak, 94.7% of Pod requests were served from warm or standby capacity. Under a two-GPU cap, the agent loop finished 13 times faster than with a new Pod per job, and the advantage disappears once jobs get long. ==Before running agent evaluation or RL, measure how much time goes to waiting for Pods.==

papers.title: Bursts That Outlast Themselves: Persistent Degradation in Prefix-Cached Agent Serving
papers.authors: Wen Huang, Jack Liu
papers.summary: Serving agents depends on the prefix cache: on a hit each turn only computes the newly added content, and on a miss the whole context of tens of thousands of tokens is recomputed. The authors find that this can drop a server into a bad state it cannot leave. With the same base traffic, a few extra minutes of burst arrivals push the vLLM cache hit ratio down to about 10%, throughput halves, and the backlog keeps growing after the burst is over. The cause is a loop: when service slows, more sessions are in flight, their combined context exceeds the KV pool, each session's prefix is evicted by other sessions before its next turn, every turn is recomputed, and service slows further. After a collapse, only blocking new requests recovered 1 run out of 7. Pausing some running sessions at turn boundaries, so that the total KV demand of active sessions stays within the pool, recovered every run within minutes. ==When serving agents, control the sessions already admitted, by KV capacity.==

papers.title: ForeSpark: Joint Draft and Verification Budget Scheduling for Parallel Speculative Decoding
papers.authors: Jaeyong Song, Daniel Wang, Pratyush Patel, Jonny Kong, Preyas Shah, Shobhit Kanaujia
papers.summary: A parallel draft model writes a whole block of draft tokens in one forward pass. Current systems write the full block first, then pick the most promising few for the target model to verify. The authors find this wasteful under high load: drafting takes up to 40% of each step, and most of what is drafted is thrown away without ever being verified. The difficulty is that a parallel draft model must fix its length before it writes, so it cannot stop when it loses confidence the way a token-by-token draft model can. Before drafting, ForeSpark uses the target model's current context features to estimate how many tokens each request would get accepted at each length, then sorts all requests in the batch together to assign both draft lengths and verification slots. On vLLM, at the same per-request generation speed, throughput is up to 1.77 times that of the strongest prior system, DSpark, with the output distribution unchanged. ==How long to draft should be decided per request before drafting==.

papers.title: One-Sided Expert-Parallel All-to-All for Mixture-of-Experts Inference over NVLink
papers.authors: Bo Li, Chulian Zhang, Or Biri, Anthony Chang, Anton Korzh, Noam Duvdevani, XingFei Xi, Daniel Stokes, Zhenhuan Chen, Lud...
papers.summary: In MoE inference every layer runs two all-to-all exchanges: first it sends tokens to the GPUs that hold their experts, then it collects the experts' outputs back. During inference each GPU handles only a few tokens at a time. The time then goes to fixed costs such as GPUs waiting on and synchronizing with each other, not to moving data. The data is small enough to cross NVLink almost instantly, yet a round trip takes tens of microseconds. NVLinkOneSided lets each GPU use only its own routing result to write tokens straight into a buffer region reserved for it on the target GPU, without first exchanging information such as token counts. The grouped GEMMs then read directly from that buffer instead of copying the tokens again in per-expert order. On Blackwell GPUs, sending plus collecting is 1.2 to 3.0 times faster than DeepEP, with the largest gains at small batches. Up to 128 tokens per GPU, the whole MoE layer is even faster than DeepGEMM MegaMoE, which fuses everything into one kernel. ==For small-batch decode communication, the cost to cut is fixed overhead, and bandwidth is not the bottleneck.==

papers.title: Inside the Trap: A Renewal Law for Prefix-Cache Collapse in LLM Agent Serving
papers.authors: Akshat Valse, Ali Jannesari
papers.summary: Multi-turn LLM agents rely on prefix caching to skip repeated work, but this paper finds a trap. After a sudden burst of sessions, an engine can fall into a state where every turn misses the cache and the backlog never drains, even at a load it handled before. In paired tests on two serving engines, two GPUs and two models, a burst of 200 sessions left the engine stuck to the end in all 30 runs, while every matched run without a burst stayed healthy. The authors model the stuck state as a queue in which every turn misses and derive how the backlog grows. The way out is simple: capping the number of concurrent sessions rescues an already trapped engine at the same load. Agent serving has to guard against bursts that wipe out the cache, not just watch average load.

papers.title: Turbocharging PiPNN for Proximity and k-NN Graph Building
papers.authors: Tobias Rubel, Richard Wen, Guy Blelloch, Laxman Dhulipala, Lars Gottesbüren, Jakub Łącki, Vahab Mirrokni
papers.summary: Graph indexes for vector search, such as HNSW and Vamana, answer queries fast but take hours or even days to build on large datasets. PiPNN speeds this up by splitting the vectors into small blocks, finding neighbors inside each block with matrix multiplication, and merging the results into one graph. This paper pushes that route further. It quantizes the vectors to low precision to cut memory traffic, and it fuses the matrix multiplication with picking the top K neighbors, so the full distance matrix is never written back to memory. On CPUs, index building is up to 8 times faster than the original PiPNN. On GPUs it is up to 50 times faster than CAGRA, with query performance at high recall matching or beating the baselines. Teams that rebuild vector indexes often may no longer be held back by build time.

papers.title: Dynamic Graph Indexing for Label-Filtered Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
papers.authors: Mengxu Jiang, Zhi Yang, Fangyuan Zhang, Yin Yang, Sibo Wang
papers.summary: Vector retrieval often comes with a filter, such as finding nearest neighbors only within a few tags or categories. The hard part is that once a graph index like HNSW is filtered by label, many edges get cut, qualifying points can no longer reach each other, and the search gets stuck locally. DYLAN arranges objects by their label sets in a prefix trie, builds shared graph indices on only some trie nodes, and puts each object into only logarithmically many indices. When a query spans several regions, it uses the graphs at ancestor nodes as bridges to jump between them. On YTB-Audio, a dataset with many labels, for queries that require all given labels, it is 43.5 times faster than the fastest baseline at recall of 0.95 or higher. Broken down, it visits 38.6 times fewer points than UNG, ==so the speedup comes from an index that lets the search walk less, not from low-level tuning==.

papers.title: e-means: outperforming k-means (in one-tenth the epochs)
papers.authors: Swann Bessa, Pierre-Emmanuel Mazaré, Gergely Szilvasy, Hugo Touvron, David Picard, Matthijs Douze, Hervé Jégou
papers.summary: Large-scale embedding clustering still often uses Lloyd's k-means, which takes many epochs and is awkward to tune. This paper turns the updates into mini-batches with an exponential moving average, and it gives scaling rules that set the decay rate and batch size from the number of clusters and the dataset size, so those knobs can be set without a hyperparameter sweep. Across embedding datasets, it reaches the loss of Lloyd k-means at 25 epochs in about two to three epochs, which translates to 10 to 45 times faster GPU wall-clock time than strong existing implementations. As one example, it partitions very large DINO embedding collections into many millions of clusters in just a few epochs, with a loss below Lloyd's longer training run.

papers.title: How We Built TLX: A Hardware-Native GPU Compiler for Production ML at Scale
papers.summary: The performance of recent GPUs depends more and more on how groups of threads divide the work, for example one group moving data while another multiplies matrices. CUDA can express this division but needs large amounts of architecture-specific orchestration code. Triton is quick to write but hides the division inside the compiler, so with each hardware generation engineers often wait for the compiler. Meta added a layer called TLX on top of Triton, so engineers keep writing Python and spell out thread-group roles and synchronization only where it matters. For recommendation engineers, the most concrete example is user features at scoring time: the same features are typically copied dozens of times to match the candidates, wasting memory bandwidth and compute with a cost that grows linearly in the number of candidates. Meta moved that copy inside the kernel and changed the model and inference runtime along with it, cutting compute-intensive net latency by up to two thirds. ==Kernel optimization is becoming a routine tool for ML engineers,== and the more candidates a model scores, the earlier this kind of change deserves a look.

papers.title: From Video Frames to Robot Meta-Frames: A Unified Latent Interface for World Action Models
papers.authors: Guoqiang Liang, Yiqi Lin, Yanzhe Chen, Kevin Yuchen Ma, Mike Zheng Shou
papers.summary: When a video diffusion model is turned into a robot world action model, low-dimensional signals such as joint state, actions and value must enter a latent space that has only seen natural video. The usual fix gives each signal its own frame, which lengthens the sequence and the attention cost. The authors first probe a frozen denoiser: signals tiled directly across the frame need large corrections, so they sit far from the video distribution, while signals packed in the frequency domain and mapped back by an inverse DCT need the smallest corrections. MetaWAM therefore splits all robot signals into separate frequency bands inside a single frame, with no new modules. On RoboCasa it reaches 68.9% success and cuts inference latency by 39%. ==How a signal is laid out in the latent space matters more than how many slots it takes.== Putting user behavior, IDs and other structured signals into an LLM token sequence raises the same question.

papers.title: Practice Makes Precise: At CoRL, NVIDIA and Partners Reveal How Robots Rehearse Delicate Work in Simulation
papers.summary: Simulation has long been where robots learn to walk, and NVIDIA now wants to use it for fine work such as aligning gears and connecting cables, where the parts are millimeter-scale and training each task separately burns GPU time without reaching high success. Among the work it presented at CoRL, AlphaNIST shows the progress best: a single policy learns every task on the NIST assembly board and receives only a success-or-failure signal during training. It reaches more than 98% training success, compared with 81% when each task gets its own policy, and uses roughly 39 times less GPU time. The sampling method behind it is plain: it favors tasks the policy succeeds at about half the time, which concentrates practice on skills still being learned. ==Training resources belong on what is only half learned==, which is what recommender engineers do when they weight hard samples.

papers.title: Real-Time Robot Execution with Masked Action Chunking
papers.authors: Haoxuan Wang, Gengyu Zhang, Yan Yan, Yuzhang Shang, Ramana Rao Kompella, Gaowen Liu
papers.summary: Running the next model call while the robot executes the current action segment is meant to avoid pauses, yet done naively it lowers success. Earlier work blamed poor joins between consecutive segments. The authors point to an overlooked cause: by the time the model finishes, the robot has already taken a few steps from the old plan, so the first steps of the new segment never run, yet training still supervises them. REMAC randomly masks the first several steps of each segment in training, computes loss only on the part that will run, and learns a LoRA correction that is merged back before inference, adding no latency. Under the largest delay in simulation, success rises from 0.451 to 0.779. ==Inference delay is a known condition, so building it into training beats patching at inference time==.

papers.title: Runway’s Praxis-1 world action model for robotics is now available
papers.summary: Runway, a video generation company, has turned its video foundation model into a robot policy called Praxis-1, released with open weights under Apache 2.0 along with inference and fine-tuning code. It is a 27B-parameter MoE diffusion Transformer that predicts upcoming frames and robot actions together. Video prediction stays in training throughout, so the model predicts the scene's next frame and then outputs the motion that gets there. Runway says web video matches teleoperated robot video as pretraining data. On RoboLab-120 it reaches 46.2% success, against 28.0% for π0.5. ==If that holds, the data bottleneck for robot policies becomes how much general video a model can learn from==.

papers.title: RoboColosseum: Evaluating Physical Intelligence at Scale In-The-Wild
papers.authors: Tan Sang Nguyen, Yi Ru Wang, Shailesh Shailesh, Gang Yang, Jiamo Hu, Jianuo Jiang, Haoquan Fang, Zhongzheng Ren, Zhongyi...
papers.summary: Ranking general-purpose robot policies is hard because real-robot experiments are difficult to reproduce: change the site or the object layout and the result changes. RoboColosseum tests five robot foundation models and three frontier LLM agents head to head on four robot types at many real sites, with both models facing the same local conditions. Frontier agents match models specialized for robots, but every system struggles to finish open-world tasks reliably. Success alone hides differences: on the G1 humanoid no policy completed any task, yet each task has several preset completion conditions and progress is the share met, and average progress still ranged from 13.3% to 23.2%. ==Rankings agree only weakly across different robots==, so evaluation should span several robots and look at progress.

papers.title: Kimodo-Policy: Learning Kinematic Action Models for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.authors: Yunheng Wang, Jiaxi Zhang, Wei Lu, Yuetong Fang, Taowen Wang, Yixiao Feng, Shuning Zhang, Junzhe Xu, Yichi Wang, Zizhao ...
papers.summary: When a humanoid walks while picking things up, its torso, arms and legs must coordinate continuously, yet existing vision-language-action and world action models inherit semantics and visual dynamics from pretraining and still have to learn body coordination downstream. This paper changes the pretraining target: it takes a text-to-motion model for the whole body as a frozen backbone and trains only small branches that feed in camera images, plus hand control. With the same structure randomly initialized and then trained, success on object-interaction tasks falls from 51.67% to 18.33%, which indicates that the inherited motion structure does help. On a real robot the mean success across eight tasks is 60%, while the lead on simulated leaderboards is small. ==With motion as the pretraining target, downstream training only has to connect the images==, the same practice as freezing a pretrained model and training only an adapter layer in recommenders.

papers.title: Learn the Task, Not the Schedule: Reducing Spurious Cross-Arm Coupling in Bimanual Imitation Learning
papers.authors: Shuyuan Hu, Deng-Ke Wu, Yifan Jin, Qianhang Luo, Mingchen Ju, Kai Ye, Bo Zhao
papers.summary: In two-armed robot demonstrations, which hand moves first is often just the operator's habit, yet imitation learning cannot separate the orderings a task requires from the ones that happened by chance, so when one arm is paused the other waits too. The authors audited four public bimanual datasets and found that tasks whose order could change rarely include more than one recorded order, and more data with the same order does not fix this. CTR cuts each arm's recording into segments and retimes them while keeping the required orderings, such as opening a drawer before placing something inside, with no new data collection. On a real robot, pausing one arm for 4 seconds costs the other arm 2.56 extra seconds under a policy trained only on concurrent-start data, and only 0.25 seconds with CTR. ==Coincidences in demonstration order get learned as signal==, and spurious correlations from exposure order in recommenders arise the same way.

papers.title: APS-VLA: Action-Guided and Future-Aware Token Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.authors: Xiaoyang Xing, Chun-Mei Feng, Anthony Cohn, Xiaoliang Gong, Asoke Nandi
papers.summary: A VLA processes hundreds of visual tokens at every step, which makes inference slow, yet the next action often depends on a small part of the image. This paper adds a small scorer in front of a frozen VLA and learns from demonstration trajectories which tokens to keep. Training asks two things: the kept tokens must let the original model produce the same action it gives with the full image, and together with the demonstrated actions they must predict how the image changes a few steps later. At deployment the scorer selects once, and the original model's weights and action generation stay unchanged. On LIBERO, pruning 75% of visual tokens makes inference 1.57 times faster while success is only 1.25 points below the unpruned model. Pruning harder barely adds speed but makes success fall faster. ==Which tokens to keep depends on whether they help the next actions and visual changes==, not only on how similar they are to the instruction. It is the same idea as learning feature selection from the downstream objective in recommendation.

papers.title: CIALLO: Learning Shared Intent Representations for Cross-Embodiment Manipulation
papers.authors: Choo Sin Wai, Dake Zhong, Jingye Zhang, Zhifang Liu, Siyao Xiao, Zirong Ding, Yuhong Zhang, Kangjie Chen, Dongbin Zhang,...
papers.summary: Robots write actions in different ways, some as joint angles and some as end-effector displacements, so one robot's demonstrations are hard to reuse on another. This paper trains an action codec that aligns actions, the change between two frames and the instruction in one space, which represents the intended motion over the next short stretch of time. Each robot's body differences live only in a small set of its own embeddings, so a new robot needs one recording of at most 10 seconds and about half an hour to update that set. A large model is then trained to predict the intent from images and instructions with only a few demonstrations per task, reaching 76.7% average success on two new real robots, compared with 70.0% for a fully finetuned off-the-shelf robot model. ==Separating body calibration from task learning lets a new robot get by with very little data.== It resembles the recommendation pattern of a shared representation plus a small set of parameters per scenario.

papers.title: Zero-Shot VLA Adaptation with Retrieved Guidance
papers.authors: Subin Kim, Anh-Quan Pham, Dinesh Jayaraman
papers.summary: Concatenating retrieved demonstrations into the model context is the standard RAG recipe for language models, but it does not carry over to robots. The authors retrieve demonstrations from real data such as DROID, whose viewpoints and objects do not match the target scene, and the context-concatenation baseline never succeeds on the real robot, doing worse than no retrieval. RAGu first warps the retrieved trajectories geometrically to the object positions in the target scene, then picks the one requiring the least change to the model's own actions. While the model generates actions, they are corrected toward that trajectory, with weights and context untouched. Real-robot success rises from 20% to 80%. ==Retrieved results need not enter the context; they can also guide generation==.
